2.1.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how is a hip implant fixed to bone?"
- "Two ways → **cement** (grout, not glue) or **biological** → **ingrowth** into pores, **on-growth** onto roughness."
- "Cement fixes in **minutes** · biological → **press-fit** first, bone fixes it over **weeks to months**."
- "Common mix → **hybrid**: cementless cup + cemented stem."

### Two methods, one goal
- **Implant fixation** = coupling the component to bone → **no motion** at the interface
[[FIG: Fig 2.1 · 2.1
- **Cement** → full fixation in theatre · **biological** → press-fit now, permanent once bone grows in
- Primary stability → **press-fit** · secondary → **osseointegration** → decides weight bearing, early vs late failure
- **Cup** → porous-coated cementless preferred · cemented → elderly, poor bone stock

| Combination | Cup | Stem |
|---|---|---|
| **Hybrid** | cementless | cemented |
| **Reverse hybrid** | cemented | cementless |

### Cemented fixation — microinterlock
- **PMMA** (polymethyl methacrylate) = **grout, not glue** → fills the space, interlocks with trabecular bone
[[FIG: Fig 2.2 · 2.1
- The **mantle** transfers load to bone · purely mechanical → **clean, dry bone** = deeper interdigitation
- Works in dense and porous bone · weakest at its **interfaces** (cement–bone, stem–cement), not the bulk

#### Reading the mantle
- **Barrack & Harris** grading → quality of the femoral mantle on the post-operative film
[[FIG: Fig 2.3 · 2.1

| Grade (Campbell) | Post-operative radiograph |
|---|---|
| **A** | complete filling → **white-out** |
| **B** | radiolucency ≤50% of the cement–bone interface |
| **C** | radiolucency 50–99%, or incomplete mantle |
| **D** | 100% radiolucency, or **no cement below the stem tip** |

- Zones → 3 Planning · loosening signs → 7 Loosening

### Biological fixation — ingrowth vs on-growth
- **Ingrowth** → endosteal bone grows **through pores** → heals like a cancellous defect
[[FIG: Fig 2.4 · 2.1
- Pores lie in the **external coating** → the solid stem stays the load-bearing core
- **On-growth** → bone grows **onto** micro-divots: **grit blasting** (aluminium oxide) or **plasma spray**
[[FIG: Fig 2.5 · 2.1
- On-growth needs a **double-wedge taper** + **press-fit**

#### Surfaces in use
| Ingrowth → porous coatings | On-growth → rough surfaces |
|---|---|
| **Sintered beads**, most popular (Ti or CoCr) · **Ti fibre mesh** | **grit-blasted** |
| Plasma-sprayed Ti alloy · **porous tantalum** · Ti foams | **plasma-sprayed** |

- Cups → commonest coating **plasma-sprayed Ti particles** · roughness alone no longer used (Prof Kamal)
[[FIG: Fig 2.6 · 2.1
- **HA** (hydroxyapatite) → osteoconductive layer over porous or grit-blasted surfaces → faster apposition
- HA closes the gap **from both sides** → less component migration
[[FIG: Fig 2.7 · 2.1

PITFALL — ingrowth or on-growth?
- Ingrowth = **into pores** of a coating · on-growth = **onto** a rough, non-porous surface
- Say → "porous coating → **ingrowth**; grit blast or plasma spray → **on-growth**; HA speeds both"

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Cement = grout, minutes · ingrowth = through pores · on-growth = onto roughness · hybrid = cementless cup + cemented stem**

2.2.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you choose cemented or cementless?"
- "Cement needs no biology → **osteoporotic, irradiated, Dorr C** bone, elderly, low demand."
- "Biological needs **living bone** and a matching canal → young, active, **Dorr A or B**."
- "Cup → **cementless** almost always, since cement fails in **shear**."

### Bone quality
- **Cement** → any bone, fills voids, needs no biology → the fallback in poor bone
- **Biological** → needs healthy bone · defeated by **osteopenia, infection, tumour, radiation**
- **Cemented stem** → elderly osteoporotic, irradiated, **Dorr C** stovepipe, deformed femur (Prof Sherif Khaled)
- Elderly osteoporotic neck fracture, Dorr C women → **cemented** stem → fewer periprosthetic fractures (Campbell)

#### The cup
- **Cementless cup** always, except poor bone → impaction may break it → cemented
- Prior **pelvic radiotherapy** → poor ingrowth, early loosening → the classic cementless trap

#### Cases (Prof Sherif Khaled)
- 36 years, **SLE** (systemic lupus) + osteoporosis → **cemented cup and stem** → fear of losing a cementless cup
[[FIG: Fig 2.8 · 2.2
- **JRA** (juvenile rheumatoid arthritis), 16 years, wheelchair-bound → **cemented**
[[FIG: Fig 2.9 · 2.2
- **RA** (rheumatoid arthritis), 30 years, good bone, suitable Dorr type → **cementless** → same disease, opposite fixation
[[FIG: Fig 2.10 · 2.2

### Stem vs cup — why cemented cups fail
- Cement → strong in **compression**, moderate in **shear**, poor in **tension**
- Stem loads cement in **compression** · cup at 30–50° inclination → **shear and tension** → voids, failure
- **Composite action** → concrete takes compression, steel rods take tension and shear (Prof Hazem)
[[FIG: Fig 2.11 · 2.2
- Hence a **cementless acetabulum** and the **hybrid hip**

PITFALL — "cement is strong, so cement the cup"?
- Cement fails in **shear**, and a cup at 30–50° loads it in shear and tension
- Say → "cement the **stem**, which works in compression; cup **cementless** unless bone is poor"

#### Outcomes & evidence
- **Cementless cup** survival → **96%** at 10 years, ≈**90%** at 20 (Prof Kamal)
- 2013 study, ≈27,000 hips → **no difference** cemented vs cementless, older designs
- Trend → more cemented in the **English National Joint Registry** (Prof Sherif Khaled)
- Literature biased → UK = cemented camp, well trained · American → few trained in cement

### Medullary canal — Dorr
- **Cement** fits any canal, even a **stovepipe** · **cementless** needs stem–endosteal contact
- Ideal → **champagne-flute** canal grips a tapered stem · a wide stovepipe gives nothing to wedge
- **Calcar-to-canal ratio** = canal width 10 cm below ÷ width at mid-lesser trochanter (Prof Fahmy)
[[FIG: Fig 2.12 · 2.2
- High ratio = thin cortices → little press-fit wedge → cement safer

| Dorr | Ratio | Films (AP + lateral) | Stem |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** champagne flute | <0.5 | thick cortices on both views | cementless · young, active |
| **B** intermediate, mild cortical flaring | 0.5–0.75 | posterior cortex thin on lateral | either, surgeon's choice |
| **C** stovepipe | >0.75 | thin cortices on both views | cemented · elderly |

- Zone of fixation → A: metaphysis · B: metaphyseal–diaphyseal · C: diaphysis, metaphysis lost
[[FIG: Fig 2.13 · 2.2
- Cementless stem in Dorr C → **undersizing, subsidence**, fracture if a fit is forced

### Khanuja classification of cementless stems
| Type (Prof Hazem) | Shape | Grips |
|---|---|---|
| **1** single wedge | broad in one plane, thin in the other | metaphysis |
| **2** double wedge | metaphyseal filling · removes much good bone | metaphysis |
| **3A** | round cone · three-point fixation · most of the market | metaphyseal–diaphyseal junction |
| **3B** Wagner | splined cone | proximal diaphysis |
| **3C** | rectangle, fully coated · four-point fixation | metaphyseal–diaphyseal junction |
| **4** | cylindrical, fully coated · diaphyseal **scratch fit** | diaphysis |
| **5** modular · **6** anatomical | separate sleeve and stem · curved | both · metaphysis |

- Khanuja 2011 → types 1–2 metaphyseal, 3 junction, 4 diaphysis
[[FIG: Fig 2.14 · 2.2

#### Types 1–2 — metaphyseal
- **Type 1** → flat wedge → depends on **correct positioning**
[[FIG: Fig 2.15 · 2.2
- **Type 2** → fills the metaphysis in both planes · impossible in Dorr A, works in Dorr C
[[FIG: Fig 2.16–2.17 · 2.2

#### Type 3 — the junction family
- **Type 3** → the stem **most surgeons** use: straight, continuous taper
[[FIG: Fig 2.18–2.19 · 2.2
- **3B Wagner** → splines give rotational stability · cone allows any version → deformed femora
[[FIG: Fig 2.20 · 2.2
- **3C** → rectangle wedges at four corners → rotational stability
[[FIG: Fig 2.21 · 2.2

#### Types 4–6 & short stems
- **Type 4** → scratch fit cracks the diaphysis → use has declined
[[FIG: Fig 2.22 · 2.2
- **Type 5** modular → metaphysis and diaphysis sized separately, e.g. S-ROM
[[FIG: Fig 2.23 · 2.2
- **Type 6** anatomical → curved to the proximal femur
[[FIG: Fig 2.24 · 2.2
- **Short stem** → ≈half a 14 cm stem, metaphyseal only · collum, partial collum, trochanter-harming
[[FIG: Fig 2.25 · 2.2

### Fixation time & weight bearing
- Fixation → cement in **minutes** · biological in **weeks to months**
- Weight bearing → cemented: **immediate full** · biological: classically **protected** → cement suits frail patients
- Modern press-fit often allows early full weight bearing → a principle, not a rule
- **Protect** weight bearing if press-fit is doubtful → **calcar crack**, poor bone

- **Poor bone → cement · Dorr A/B young → cementless · cup cementless (shear) · Khanuja: fixation area grows with type**

2.3.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is bone cement made of?"
- "Powder → PMMA + **benzoyl peroxide** initiator · liquid → **monomer** + **DMPT** activator."
- "Mixing → **exothermic** polymerisation: 80–86 °C in vitro, ≈40–47 °C in the body."
- "Insert in the **working phase** · antibiotic only if **heat-stable** powder."

### Composition & reaction
- Powder and liquid kept apart → no premature polymerisation
[[FIG: Fig 2.26 · 2.3
- Liquid monomer alone → long setting, big heat, **shrinkage** → hence **pre-polymerised powder**
- **Exothermic** → in vitro 80–86 °C · in vivo **40–47 °C**: thin layer, stem, blood flow, water (Prof Fahmy)
[[FIG: Fig 2.27 · 2.3
- Thick cement masses → hottest · monomer volatile, irritant → **closed vacuum mixing** protects staff

| Powder | Agent | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Polymer | **PMMA** | scaffold |
| Initiator | **benzoyl peroxide** | free radicals |
| Radiopacifier | **barium sulfate** or zirconium dioxide (Surgery of the Hip) | visible on X-ray |
| Antibiotic, optional | heat-stable **gentamicin**, tobramycin, vancomycin | local prophylaxis |

| Liquid | Agent | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Monomer | **methyl methacrylate** | polymerises |
| Activator = accelerator | **DMPT** (dimethyl-p-toluidine) | splits benzoyl peroxide at room temperature |
| Inhibitor | **hydroquinone** | shelf life |
| Colorant | chlorophyll (green) · methylene blue | shows excess cement |

#### Antibiotic cement
- Must be **heat-stable**, water-soluble, powder → survives setting heat, still leaches out
- More powder → weaker cement → **delivery vs strength**
- Commercial packs carry **<1 g** per 40 g → a spacer needs added drug

PITFALL — how much antibiotic per 40 g?
- Fixation **≤1 g** (Miller) · spacer **3–4 g** · Campbell → 2–4 g vancomycin ± 1.2 g tobramycin
- Say → "**≤1 g to fix · ≤4 g (<10%) in a spacer · never >8 g**" (Prof Abdel Moneim)

### Working phases
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Dough time** | mixing → no longer sticks to gloves |
| **Working time** | dough → hardened · the stem goes in |
| **Setting time** | mixing → hardening = **dough + working time** |
| Low viscosity | long dough, short working → sets fast |
| High viscosity | short dough, long working → sets slowly |

- Warm theatre or components → all phases shorter · cold → longer
- Insert in the **working phase** → stiff enough to resist bleeding, fluid enough to interdigitate
- Stem proud after an early set → accept, or remove all cement and redo · **never hammer**

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Powder = PMMA + benzoyl peroxide + barium · liquid = monomer + DMPT + hydroquinone · setting = dough + working**

2.4.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "cemented or cementless — pros and cons?"
- "Cement → any bone, any canal, **immediate** fixation, cheaper · but **brittle**, static, heat and **BCIS** risk."
- "Biological → a **living interface** that repairs itself for decades · needs good bone, regular canal."
- "Price of cementless → **stress shielding** and **periprosthetic fracture**."

### Cemented — where it earns its place
- Ideal → **osteoporotic, irradiated** bone · any canal · sets in minutes · easier, standard stem, **cheaper**
- Survival → **97%** at 10 years, **89%** at 15 (Prof Sherif Khaled)
- Suits → rheumatological disease, older, osteoporotic, **Dorr C**, low activity
- **Tumour** adjuvant → after curettage of a giant cell tumour, PMMA fills the cavity, heat kills residual cells

#### How cement fails
- **Static, brittle** interface → cracks never repair → abrupt failure, no plastic deformation
[[FIG: Fig 2.28 · 2.4
- **Notch-sensitive** → a notch is a **stress riser** · at revision → crack the cement first
- Long term → **creep**, **stress relaxation**, **fatigue failure**
[[FIG: Fig 2.29 · 2.4
- Fatigue → below ultimate strength, cyclic load, high-stress points · stress relaxation protects

#### Local & systemic risk
- Local **thermal injury** and necrosis · high failure of **cemented cups**
- Pressurisation → marrow and fat **emboli** + monomer **vasodilation** → hypotension, hypoxia, bradycardia, arrest
- **BCIS** (bone cement implantation syndrome) → frail fracture patients most at risk → warn the anaesthetist
- Prevention → **lavage**, canal **venting**, haemodynamic monitoring

### Biological — what ingrowth offers
- **Dynamic** interface → new bone repairs minor defects → remodels for decades
- Age **15** → cementless · cement only by a surgeon trained in good technique, as in the UK (Prof Sherif Khaled)
[[FIG: Fig 2.30 · 2.4

#### Costs & complications
- Needs a regular canal (**Dorr A**) · not porous or irradiated bone · fixation takes weeks to months
- **Proximal coating** → loads metaphysis · **extensive** → loads diaphysis → proximal **stress shielding**
[[FIG: Fig 2.31 · 2.4
- More **periprosthetic fracture** → press-fit vs line-to-line, extensive coating
- **Calcar crack** on broaching → consider a prophylactic **cerclage wire**

#### Signs of a well-fixed cementless implant
- Spot welds, load bypass, Engh grades → 7 Loosening

### Enhancing biological fixation
- **Porous ingrowth** beats grit-blasted on-growth → aim: strengthen on-growth
- Needs **immediate mechanical stability** + intimate bone contact
[[FIG: Fig 2.32 · 2.4
- Bone grows only on a **still** surface → less early micromotion

| Strategy | How |
|---|---|
| 1 · More surface | extensive coating |
| 2 · Initial stability | **press-fit** rather than line-to-line |
| 3 · Extra hold | **screws** for grit-blasted cups |

- Strategies 1 and 2 also raised fracture risk → stability vs bone damage

#### Press-fit in practice
- **Press-fit** → under-reamed, rim compressed · cup needs no screws
[[FIG: Fig 2.33 · 2.4
- **Line-to-line** → cup needs screws · stem extensively coated for a frictional fit
- Under-ream the rim **1–2 mm** · press-fit better · poor fit → add **screws** (Prof Kamal)
- Excessive under-reaming → **acetabular fracture** or dome gap → check via the **apical hole**

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Cement: immediate, brittle, BCIS · biological: self-repairing, shielding, fracture · press-fit = under-ream 1–2 mm**

### Cementing generations
| Generation | Canal | Mixing · delivery | Centralisation |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1st** | rasps, suction, gauze · femoral-head bone plug or none | hand · **finger packing** | distal only |
| **2nd** | brush, sponge, pre-made **plug** | hand · retrograde **cement gun** | proximal + distal |
| **3rd** | **pulsed lavage**, brush, drying | **vacuum** or centrifuge · gun + **pressuriser**, rubber seal | proximal + distal |
| **4th**, some texts | as 3rd | as 3rd | + precoated or roughened stem |

- 1st generation → no preparation, plug or pressure → blood and void inclusions
[[FIG: Fig 2.34 · 2.5
- Each step fixes a failure → air bubbles start cracks · off-centre stem → thin mantle cracks first
- **Restrictor** ≈**1–2 cm** below the planned stem tip → mantle passes the tip (Campbell)
- **Varus** stem → thin mantle **proximal-medial** and **distal-lateral**

### Determinants of biological fixation
- Like fracture healing → living bone, right scaffold, small gap, **stability** → failure = stability or contact missing

| Factor | Target |
|---|---|
| Pore size · depth | **50–400 µm** (Prof Fahmy) · deeper = more penetration |
| Porosity | **40–50%** best |
| Gap to bone | **<50 µm** |
| Micromotion | bone **<50 µm** · fibrous tissue **>150 µm** (Miller) |
| Bone | viable · irradiation → aseptic loosening |

- **Ra** (average peak-to-valley) of an on-growth surface → higher = better grip
[[FIG: Fig 2.35 · 2.5
- Ream so the implant rests on **cortical**, not cancellous bone · **initial rigid fixation** is critical
- Stable fibrous vs loose stem → 7 Loosening

PITFALL — how much micromotion is allowed?
- Old notes → bone <40 µm · Miller → bone **<50 µm**, fibrous **>150 µm**
- Say → "**under 50 µm bone grows in · over 150 µm a fibrous membrane forms**"

### Cement strength — what weakens, what helps
| Weakens | Strengthens |
|---|---|
| time (static interface) · moisture | good design · **centralisation** |
| blood, tissue inclusions | **vacuum or centrifuge mixing** → no air voids |
| excess additives: antibiotic, barium | **pressurisation** → compaction |
| stem moved while setting · high-speed mixing | lower body temperature |
| thin mantle | |

- Roots → contamination, porosity, mechanics · moving the stem breaks the cement–stem bond → hold still

#### The mantle
- Avoid failure → **>2 mm**, uniform, low porosity, pressurised, clean dry bone, stiff stem, no sharp edges (Prof Fahmy)
- Ideal femoral mantle → ≈**4 mm proximally**, **2 mm distally** (Campbell)
- Stresses → compression in the mantle · **shear + tension** at the cement–metal interface · voids weaken

- **Cemented cup** → PMMA spacers **3 mm** high → uniform **≈3 mm** mantle [Prof Kamal 2–4 mm, ≈2.5] (Campbell)

### Composite beam vs loaded taper
| | **Composite beam** | **Loaded taper** = taper-slip |
|---|---|---|
| Surface · shape | rough · anatomical · collar favoured | **polished** · tapered · collarless · void at tip |
| Concept | **bonded** to cement → initial stability | **subsides** ≈1 mm in year 1 → secondary stability |
| Weak point | not forgiving · any micromotion → cracks | a collar blocks subsidence |
| Example | — | **Exeter** |

- Two philosophies, opposite logic

[[FIG: Fig 2.39 · 2.5
- Loaded taper → inserted with a **hollow centraliser** at the tip

- **Controlled subsidence** → the wedge tightens in its mantle

#### Why subsidence works
- Subsidence → **radial compression** in cement → tensile **hoop stress** in bone (Prof Fahmy)
[[FIG: Fig 2.42 · 2.5
- **Creep** increases interdigitation · **stress relaxation** dissipates bone tension at rest

CLINICAL PEARL — never mix the concepts
- A **collar** on a polished taper blocks subsidence → harmful (Prof Hazem)
- Polished, collarless, tapered → loaded taper · rough, collared → composite beam

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "where do you put acetabular screws?"

### Indications & costs
- Screws → stability when fixation is poor · **periprosthetic fracture** · **revision** → a tool, not routine
- Needs a **modular** shell · a **monoblock** cup takes no screws (Prof Kamal)
[[FIG: Fig 2.43 · 2.6
- Costs → **wear particles**, fretting corrosion, neurovascular injury · each screw = a debris path
- Unused holes → **hole eliminators** → less debris reaching the pelvis

### The quadrant system
- **Wasielewski** → line A: **ASIS** (anterior superior iliac spine) → acetabular centre → posterior fovea (Campbell)
[[FIG: Fig 2.44 · 2.6
- Line B → **perpendicular** to line A at the centre → four quadrants
- Course variant → ASIS–ischium line + perpendicular → screws in the superior zone
- Abnormal version or **high hip centre** shifts quadrants → only the peripheral posterior halves are safe (Campbell)

| Zone | Quadrant | At risk · rule |
|---|---|---|
| **Safe** | posterosuperior | sciatic nerve, superior gluteal nerve and vessels · strong bone → screws **>25 mm** (Campbell) |
| **Caution** | posteroinferior | sciatic nerve, inferior gluteal and pudendal vessels · bone ≈25 mm → screws ≤**20 mm** (Prof Khaled Fawzy) |
| **Danger** | anteroinferior | obturator nerve and vessels |
| **Death** | anterosuperior | **external iliac** artery and vein |

- Anterior vessels lie on the inner wall with no soft-tissue cover → injury may show late
[[FIG: Fig 2.45 · 2.6
- **Corona mortis** → obturator–external iliac or epigastric anastomosis over the superior ramus → catastrophic bleeding
- Technique → depth gauge, hand-controlled drill, feel the far cortex, prefer posterosuperior holes
